claude_take: What ties today's stories together is how much of the current AI and media boom runs on relationships of trust that are suddenly being tested: Nvidia's board is investigating whether its own CEO's personal life compromised national security, and OpenAI is yanking model access from a company the instant its ownership changes hands. Meanwhile the less glamorous infrastructure underneath all this ambition is buckling under plainer pressure: Skydance is funding its $6 billion in promised savings with real-estate and marketing cuts rather than creative confidence, and a 188-year-old department store folded over an unpaid rent bill. Even as AI capability keeps getting cheaper, see Meta's new bargain-rate agent model, the institutions built on top of it are held together by contracts and loyalty that look more fragile by the week.
claude_take_title: Held Together by Contracts, Not Confidence

items.headline: Nvidia's Board Investigation Into CEO Jensen Huang Escalates to Congress
items.summary: Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation after Jensen Huang admitted to a relationship with a businesswoman US intelligence reportedly considers a Chinese intelligence asset; the company says it has found no evidence trade secrets were compromised and that Huang retains its backing. House Republican committee chairs have asked Huang for a closed-door briefing on his contacts with her and on Nvidia's defenses against foreign espionage, with a session floated for November 18, and Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott has separately asked Huang and Commerce Secretary Lutnick to testify. The episode is landing just as Washington debates tightening export controls on AI chips to China, raising the stakes for the company sitting at the center of the AI buildout's supply chain.

items.headline: OpenAI Cuts Off Cursor's Access to Its Models After SpaceX's Acquisition
items.summary: OpenAI's planned wind-down of direct model access for the AI coding tool Cursor took effect November 12, following SpaceX's acquisition of Cursor's parent company. OpenAI says it can't be confident SpaceX will honor its usage terms, pointing to past violations by X and xAI, both now under the same ownership, and says it won't offer future models, including its upcoming 'Astra,' to Cursor while SpaceX owns it. Cursor says OpenAI models accounted for only about 5% of its traffic and that it still offers Anthropic, Google and xAI models, but the move is a stark example of how access to frontier AI models is becoming a tool of corporate rivalry rather than a straightforward commercial relationship.

items.headline: Meta Releases Muse Ember, a Low-Cost Model Built for AI Agent Workloads
items.summary: Meta released Muse Ember, its smallest and most efficient model yet, built to handle the repetitive subtasks inside AI agent systems, such as reading screenshots, parsing documents, or routing requests, while pairing with a larger model like Meta's own Muse Wonder for harder reasoning. It is multimodal, taking in text, images, video, audio and PDFs, with adjustable reasoning effort and pricing starting at a fraction of a cent per task. The release reflects a broader shift among AI labs toward cheap, specialized 'worker' models that make agentic systems affordable to run at scale, rather than routing every small step through an expensive frontier model.

items.headline: Skydance Targets $6 Billion in Cost Cuts, Plans to Merge HBO Max and Paramount+
items.summary: In its first earnings report since closing the $81 billion Warner Bros. Discovery takeover, Skydance-owned Paramount posted a modest Q3 profit and laid out a plan to cut roughly $6 billion in costs over three years, with the bulk of the savings front-loaded into year one through corporate overhead, real estate and marketing cuts. The company confirmed it won't spin off Warner's cable assets and will bundle HBO Max with Paramount+ starting early 2027, eventually merging them into one service. Analysts remain skeptical the targeted savings are enough to offset the roughly $80-90 billion in debt taken on for the deal, and the company warned Warner's film slate will weigh on Q4 results.

items.headline: Amanda Seyfried's Documentary Role Exposes a Gap in Awards-Season Rules
items.summary: Amanda Seyfried's performance in the documentary 'You Can See Everything' has made her eligible for a Critics Choice Award but shut out of the Golden Globes, BAFTA and the Screen Actors Guild Awards, none of which recognize documentary performances at all. No documentary performance has ever been nominated by a major acting body, and the gap is drawing fresh attention as documentaries increasingly use reenactments and performed scenes to tell true stories, blurring the line with narrative filmmaking. It's a small story, but one that points to awards infrastructure struggling to keep pace with how documentaries are actually being made today.

items.headline: COP31 Climate Talks Reach a Tense Final Stretch Over Money and Fossil Fuels
items.summary: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, entered its final days of negotiation still split over who pays for the energy transition and whether fossil fuels get a defined phase-out path. Developing nations are pressing rich countries for firmer climate-finance commitments, European countries are pushing a global electrification pact, and fossil-fuel producers are resisting language that would commit them to winding down oil, gas and coal; UN Secretary-General António Guterres used his address to call for taxing fossil fuel companies to fund climate damage elsewhere. With talks scheduled to wrap this week, negotiators are still far from a deal, underscoring how little consensus exists on who should bear the cost of a crisis almost everyone agrees is real.

items.headline: David Jones, Australia's 188-Year-Old Department Store, Collapses Into Administration
items.summary: David Jones entered voluntary administration on November 5 after its owner, Anchorage Capital Partners, stopped paying rent at its Westfield stores and talks with landlord Scentre Group broke down. Administrators from McGrathNicol are now seeking a buyer or recapitalization while roughly 6,000 staff across 38 stores in Australia and New Zealand keep working amid uncertainty over store closures before Christmas. The collapse of a 188-year-old retail institution, done in by a straightforward rent dispute rather than a shift in taste, is a stark marker of how much pressure legacy department stores are under even when their brand recognition remains intact.

items.headline: Sartre's Bad Faith
items.summary: Jean-Paul Sartre argued that human beings are 'condemned to be free': unlike objects with a fixed nature, we have no essence dictating what we must do, so every choice is genuinely ours, with no excuse to hide behind. 'Bad faith' is the self-deception by which people deny this freedom, telling themselves their role, their nature, or their circumstances left them no choice, in order to escape the anxiety that comes with full responsibility. The idea remains a sharp lens on modern life, where people routinely explain away their choices through job titles, algorithms, or 'that's just who I am,' treating freedom as a burden to offload rather than a condition to own.
items.summary_fr: Jean-Paul Sartre soutenait que l'être humain est « condamné à être libre » : contrairement aux objets, dotés d'une nature fixe, nous n'avons aucune essence qui nous dicterait quoi faire, si bien que chaque choix nous appartient entièrement, sans excuse possible. La « mauvaise foi » désigne cette auto-tromperie par laquelle on nie sa propre liberté, en se persuadant que notre rôle, notre nature ou les circonstances ont décidé à notre place, afin d'échapper à l'angoisse qu'implique une responsabilité pleine et entière. Cette idée reste un outil incisif pour lire la vie contemporaine, où l'on explique sans cesse ses choix par un statut professionnel, un algorithme ou un « c'est comme ça que je suis », traitant la liberté comme un fardeau à décharger plutôt que comme une condition à assumer.
